edition.deck: Israel votes in a closely contested election as fighting pauses for aid and evacuation in occupied Ukraine. In the UK, tomorrow’s Budget looms over business and household concerns; in Denmark, fresh legal and workplace developments make the news.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises fresh developments and consequential reporting. Returning Israel coverage earns a place through election-day turnout and new reporting from Hebron; the Lula election story is not repeated without a comparable new development.

content.headline: Israelis vote in tight election as Hebron families face displacement
content.shortHeadline: Israel votes as Hebron families face displacement
content.standfirst: Turnout is at a record level in Israel’s first election since the 7 October attacks, with no clear path to a governing majority. In Hebron, families displaced by military restrictions say they do not know when they can return.

image.caption: A screen in Tel Aviv shows Benjamin Netanyahu and rival Gadi Eisenkot ahead of the election.

sources.originalTitle: Turnout so far highest on record as Israelis vote in pivotal election
Et dødeligt angreb har ført til nedlukning for en kvart million mennesker: ‘Det er kollektiv afstraffelse’

segments.body: Israelis are voting in an election widely seen as a referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu. Turnout so far is at a record level, but polling cited by the BBC suggests neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition can secure the 61 seats needed for a majority. Coalition negotiations could take weeks or months.

segments.title: Hebron under restrictions
segments.body: In Hebron, DR reports that Israeli forces have closed routes in and out of the city after an attack that killed two Israeli soldiers. A local official said about 1,200 people had been ordered to leave their homes; a displaced resident told DR he did not know whether his family would be allowed back. Israel says its operations target militants and weapons; Palestinian officials and residents describe the restrictions and demolitions as collective punishment.

content.headline: Oleshky truce opens a narrow window for aid and civilian evacuation
content.shortHeadline: Oleshky truce offers a narrow window for aid and evacuation
content.standfirst: A limited ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city is intended to let supplies in and civilians out. Residents face severe shortages, while the safety, route and practical arrangements for evacuation remain uncertain.

sources.originalTitle: Truce begins in Ukraine city where residents ate weeds to survive
Oleshky truce appears to hold as two European leaders have ‘frank’ call with Putin

segments.body: A limited truce has begun in Oleshky, where residents have been trapped without reliable food, water or electricity. Ukrainian officials and Russia’s defence ministry say it is being observed. The BBC reports that the pause is due to last until 1 November, with aid deliveries and an evacuation planned for Friday.

segments.title: Risks remain
segments.body: Residents have told the BBC they are suffering extreme hunger, with some cooking garden weeds. Roads out of the city are mined and exposed to drone attacks. Ukrainian officials warn that people leaving may be taken towards Russia or occupied Crimea; the detailed routes and arrangements have not been fully established, and reports from inside the city are difficult to verify.

content.headline: Nordic leaders’ Putin call exposes Europe’s divide over direct talks
content.shortHeadline: Putin call exposes Europe’s divide over direct talks
content.standfirst: Finland’s president and Norway’s prime minister held a rare 90-minute conversation with Russia’s leader about diplomacy and Ukraine. Denmark’s prime minister says the initiative was not coordinated and risks giving Putin renewed legitimacy.

sources.originalTitle: Norway and Finland leaders hold rare call with Putin
ANALYSE Opsigtsvækkende Putin-samtale rusker op i følsom debat i Europa

segments.body: Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre say they called Vladimir Putin to discuss Russia’s war against Ukraine and possible negotiations. They said they were acting as leaders of their own countries, not on behalf of Europe. Støre described the exchange as substantive but said there were major differences in views.

perspectives.body: DR’s analysis focuses on the diplomatic rift: Mette Frederiksen argues European countries should speak with one voice and warns that direct contact could bring Putin back into the political mainstream. Støre, by contrast, says neighbouring countries have a responsibility to pursue their own interests.

segments.title: A question of representation
segments.body: The call followed meetings with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo, and was linked to planned trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi. Frederiksen says the Nordic initiative was not agreed with other European leaders. The question of who, if anyone, should represent Europe in negotiations remains unresolved.

content.headline: Trump faces familiar cost-of-living test as prices outpace wages
content.shortHeadline: Trump faces a familiar cost-of-living test
content.standfirst: US growth and employment figures remain relatively strong, but prices are still rising faster than wages. The BBC’s analysis says voters’ experience of everyday costs may outweigh the economic indicators ahead of the midterms.

image.caption: Donald Trump and former president Joe Biden.

sources.originalTitle: Donald Trump's biggest economic problem looks strangely familiar

segments.body: The latest inflation report confirms that prices remain high, despite solid economic growth, low unemployment and a near-record stock market. Average hourly earnings rose 3% over the past year, while consumer prices increased 3.7%, leaving many households feeling the squeeze.

segments.title: The political risk
segments.body: Trump promised swift relief from rising prices, but some economists attribute part of the increase to his tariffs and the higher energy costs linked to the US-Israel conflict with Iran. The White House points to growth, investment and tax cuts as evidence its policies are working. The BBC notes that voters often judge the economy by bills and shopping costs rather than headline data.

content.headline: Comey denies new charges over alleged 2016 disclosure
content.shortHeadline: Comey denies new charges over alleged disclosure
content.standfirst: The former FBI director says the case is politically motivated and has asked a judge to dismiss it. The allegations remain under seal, and his lawyers argue the prosecution may have missed the statute-of-limitations deadline.

sources.originalTitle: Ex-FBI chief James Comey faces federal charges for third time

segments.body: Federal prosecutors have filed two charges against former FBI director James Comey over an alleged disclosure of national defence information to The New York Times in 2016, according to court papers described by his lawyers. Comey denies wrongdoing and calls the case an abuse of the justice system.

segments.title: Legal challenge
segments.body: The charges were filed through a criminal information rather than a grand-jury indictment. Comey’s lawyers have moved to dismiss the case, arguing that two earlier investigative teams decided not to prosecute and that the 10-year statute of limitations may have expired. A former federal prosecutor cited by the BBC said the time limit could strengthen the dismissal motion; the allegations themselves remain under seal.

content.headline: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals losses, risks and dependence on computing
content.shortHeadline: Anthropic filing lays bare losses and AI risks
content.standfirst: The company behind Claude disclosed fast-growing revenue alongside enormous losses, infrastructure costs and dependence on a small group of customers. Its filing also warns that advanced AI could pose catastrophic risks without safeguards.

image.caption: Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei.

sources.originalTitle: Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know

segments.body: Anthropic’s 335-page stock-market filing says the company lost $80.7bn in the first half of the year while bringing in $16.2bn in revenue. It has not set a target share price. The company also disclosed substantial commitments to data-centre capacity and reliance on a small number of large customers.

segments.title: Risks set out by the company
segments.body: Anthropic warned that advanced AI could pose catastrophic or existential risks if developed or deployed without appropriate safeguards. It also described a cyberattack it attributed to a group it believes was sponsored by China. These are disclosures and assessments made by the company in its own filing, alongside its claims about AI’s potential benefits.

content.headline: FBI raids California home linked to investigation of Eric Swalwell
content.shortHeadline: FBI raids home linked to Swalwell investigation
content.standfirst: The Justice Department confirmed an FBI operation in the Los Angeles region but gave no further details. The former congressman has denied sexual misconduct allegations that are the subject of the ongoing investigation.

image.caption: Eric Swalwell left the California governor’s race earlier this year.

sources.originalTitle: FBI raids California home tied to former Congressman Eric Swalwell - US media

segments.body: The FBI raided a California home connected to an ongoing criminal investigation involving former congressman Eric Swalwell, according to US media reports. The Justice Department confirmed an FBI operation in the Los Angeles region but did not identify the subject or provide details.

segments.title: Investigation continues
segments.body: Swalwell left Congress and ended his California governor campaign after multiple women made sexual misconduct allegations, which he has denied; his lawyer has called them fabricated. The BBC says the FBI previously seized his electronic devices and searched his Washington home. The allegations have not been established in court.

content.headline: Rare Nanotyrannus skeleton sells for $47.3m amid public-access debate
content.shortHeadline: Nanotyrannus fossil sells for $47.3m
content.standfirst: The New York auction followed recent research identifying the fossil as a distinct dinosaur genus. Scientists say a private sale could put a rare specimen beyond public view, while another palaeontologist says such fossils may eventually reach museums.

sources.originalTitle: Nanotyrannus skeleton auctioned for $47.3m in New York

segments.body: A roughly 10-foot Nanotyrannus skeleton known as Jodi sold at Sotheby’s in New York for $47.3m, far above its expected price of at least $9m. The buyer’s identity has not been disclosed. Researchers confirmed the genus was distinct from Tyrannosaurus rex last year.

segments.title: Who gets to study the fossil?
segments.body: Palaeontologist Steve Brusatte called the sale harrowing, warning that the specimen could disappear into a private collection and be unavailable for research or public display. Megan Jenkins said she understood why those involved wanted to sell it and thought many such finds ultimately enter public view. The buyer’s plans are unknown.

content.headline: Budget expected to raise minimum wage, but younger workers get smaller rise
content.shortHeadline: Budget wage rise for younger workers set to slow
content.standfirst: The proposed increase for 18-to-20-year-olds is smaller than in the past two years, while remaining below the adult rate. The Budget also includes measures on carers’ allowance and import tariffs as households face cost pressures.

sources.originalTitle: Minimum wage set to rise but 18-20 year-olds will not get bigger increase

segments.body: The Budget is expected to raise the minimum wage, but the increase for workers aged 18 to 20 is set to be smaller than in the previous two years. The BBC reports that the government’s pledge to equalise adult rates over time remains, while ministers say the change must account for pressures on employers.

segments.title: Other cost-of-living measures
segments.body: The government says removing import tariffs on some food and other products could save households up to £21 a year, and it plans to change carers’ allowance so a small rise in earnings no longer triggers the loss of a full week’s payment. Unions say different minimum rates for the same work are unfair; the Conservatives argue the measures will not offset rising costs.

content.headline: UK businesses in significant financial distress reach a 20-year high
content.shortHeadline: Business distress reaches a 20-year high
content.standfirst: A report by administrator BTG counts 738,144 firms in significant distress, with hospitality particularly hard hit. The figures add to pressure on the chancellor to address rising costs and arrears in Wednesday’s Budget.

image.caption: A bar and restaurant, among the businesses facing financial pressure.

sources.originalTitle: Number of UK businesses in financial distress ‘at two-decade high’

segments.body: BTG says 738,144 UK businesses were in significant financial distress in the third quarter, the highest figure since its report began in 2004. The total was 1.6% higher than a year earlier. Hospitality had the sharpest increase among the sectors highlighted, with the number of bars and restaurants in distress up 5% to 18,866.

segments.title: Mounting costs and tax arrears
segments.body: BTG chief executive Mark Fry cites higher employment costs, inflation, energy bills and borrowing costs. The firm also found that businesses owed HMRC £27.3bn in VAT, corporation tax and PAYE arrears at the end of August. These figures come from BTG’s report and information request; they do not establish the condition of every UK business.

content.headline: Budget debate pits carbon-capture funding against household heat-pump grants
content.shortHeadline: Budget puts carbon capture and heat-pump grants in focus
content.standfirst: Chris Packham and campaigners want less public money for carbon capture and stronger support for heat pumps. Installers warn that any subsidy cuts could threaten jobs and a young UK industry; the government has not confirmed its Budget plans.

image.caption: Ed Miliband visits the Acorn carbon-capture project in Aberdeenshire.

sources.originalTitle: UK spending on ‘fairytale’ carbon capture tech is a national embarrassment, chancellor told
‘No one saves the planet if it hits their pocket’: UK heat pump installers fear planned subsidy cuts

segments.body: Chris Packham is urging the chancellor to reconsider £24bn earmarked for carbon capture and storage, arguing that funding should go to measures that reliably cut emissions and household bills. Campaigners say costly projects have often struggled to deliver expected carbon savings; the Carbon Capture and Storage Association says existing projects have already generated supply-chain contracts and could support thousands of construction jobs.

perspectives.body: The Carbon Capture and Storage Association argues that pulling back from existing projects would weaken investor confidence, risk leaving infrastructure underused and damage industrial prospects.

segments.title: Heat-pump support under scrutiny
segments.body: The Guardian reports that grants of up to £9,000 under the boiler upgrade scheme may be reduced in Wednesday’s Budget, though the government has not confirmed a change. Installers say many customers rely on the grants and warn abrupt cuts could harm businesses, employment and UK manufacturing. The government says it remains committed to clean energy and warmer homes.

content.headline: UK households buy emergency supplies after government preparedness advice
content.shortHeadline: Emergency-supply sales rise after government advice
content.standfirst: Some retailers report higher sales of tinned food, water, torches and radios after a campaign urged households to prepare for 72 hours without services. Other supermarkets say demand has not materially changed and that supplies remain strong.

image.caption: Supermarkets say supplies of long-life food remain strong.

sources.originalTitle: Bottled water and tinned food sales surge after UK government issues emergency stockpile advice

segments.body: The government’s Be Ready campaign has prompted reported sales increases at some retailers. Iceland said tinned-food sales were up 40% over the weekend, while Maplin reported a near fourfold rise in torch sales and doubled sales of power banks and radios. Specialist preparedness shops also reported shortages of some items.

segments.title: No sign of general shortages
segments.body: The response has not been uniform: several major supermarkets reported no material change in demand. The British Retail Consortium says food availability remains strong and retailers are well stocked with essentials. The campaign advises households to keep supplies for 72 hours; the reporting does not suggest that the country is facing a shortage of these goods.

content.headline: Prosecutor says four men believed they could rely on husband’s consent
content.shortHeadline: Court hears four men deny assaulting Joanne Young
content.standfirst: The trial concerns allegations that four men sexually assaulted Joanne Young while she was sedated and restrained. Her former husband has pleaded guilty to abuse; the four defendants deny the charges and say they believed she consented.

image.caption: One of the defendants arrives at Winchester Crown Court.

sources.originalTitle: Woman’s world ‘tilted on axis’ on learning husband invited men to sexually assault her, court told

segments.body: Winchester Crown Court has heard that Philip Young advertised his then-wife Joanne on websites and invited men to sexually assault her while she was sedated, restrained and blindfolded. Young has pleaded guilty to multiple abuse charges. Four men jointly charged with assaulting her deny the allegations.

segments.title: The question of consent
segments.body: Prosecutor Sarah Jones told the jury that the defendants are expected to argue they believed Joanne Young was consenting. She said the case will examine whether it could be reasonable to rely on another person’s claim of consent without checking with the woman herself. The trial is ongoing; the defendants’ guilt has not been determined.

content.headline: British politicians barred from West Bank visit to meet Palestinian communities
content.shortHeadline: British MPs among delegates barred from West Bank
content.standfirst: Four elected representatives were among an international delegation stopped at the Allenby crossing while travelling to meet Palestinian civil society and olive growers. Israel has been contacted for comment; the reported reason for refusing entry was not given.

image.caption: British MPs Clive Lewis and Lara Bird were among the delegates barred from the West Bank.

sources.originalTitle: British politicians among international delegates barred from entering West Bank

segments.body: An international delegation of 23 people, including British MPs Clive Lewis and Lara Bird, says it was detained for nine hours and barred from entering the West Bank. The group had planned to attend a gathering in Ramallah and meet Palestinian academics, community leaders and farmers during the olive harvest.

segments.title: Dispute over access
segments.body: Delegates said they were given no reason for the refusal. Lewis described being questioned, while Bird said she had planned to stand alongside Palestinians harvesting olives. The Guardian reports that the UN recorded at least 160 settler attacks linked to the harvest in the first two weeks of October. Israel’s embassy was contacted for comment.

content.headline: Burnham’s EU remarks deepen Labour divisions over freedom of movement
content.shortHeadline: Burnham’s EU remarks expose Labour divisions
content.standfirst: The prime minister says Britain should have an honest discussion about its long-term relationship with Europe, while insisting he is not proposing a return to free movement now. Labour MPs and ministers remain divided over the issue and its electoral risks.

image.caption: Andy Burnham speaks in an ITV interview about Britain’s relationship with Europe.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Mahmood is furious’: Cabinet anger as Burnham opens door to Brexit free movement
‘It only boosts Farage’: Red Wall MPs fear return of EU freedom of movement

segments.body: Andy Burnham’s comments about a possible future return to EU freedom of movement have angered some cabinet colleagues, including Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, who says an open discussion is not settled government policy. Downing Street says Burnham has not proposed a specific option and that the public would decide.

segments.title: Different views within Labour
segments.body: Some Labour MPs in Brexit-voting areas warn that reopening the issue could strengthen Reform UK and revive political divisions. Others, including MP Andy McDonald and pro-European Labour campaigners, say closer cooperation with the EU should be considered. The disagreement extends to whether any future change would require a referendum.

perspectives.body: The reporting records opposition among Red Wall MPs alongside support from other Labour figures, showing that the dispute is not simply a contest between the government and Reform UK.

content.headline: Suffolk village votes for symbolic ‘leave the UK’ referendum over asylum plan
content.shortHeadline: Suffolk village backs symbolic vote over asylum site
content.standfirst: Barnham residents voted 73 to seven to hold a symbolic referendum over plans to house up to 930 asylum seekers at a former RAF base. The Home Office says it is engaging with local authorities and says the sites would be self-contained and secure.

image.caption: A former RAF site in Suffolk is proposed for asylum accommodation.

sources.originalTitle: Inside the Suffolk village set to follow Piddington and vote to leave the UK

segments.body: Residents of Barnham, Suffolk, have voted to hold a symbolic referendum on the government’s plan to use RAF Barnham for asylum accommodation. The Home Office has reduced its proposed capacity from 1,250 to 930 people. The village has a population of about 600, according to the report.

segments.title: Local concerns and official response
segments.body: Residents quoted by the i Paper express differing views: some oppose the plan over security and community concerns, while another said asylum seekers had been treated unfairly during disorder in nearby Thetford. The council leader has raised concerns about protected birds. The Home Office says former military sites are intended to be self-contained, with round-the-clock security and CCTV.

content.headline: Norwegian to cut 123 Copenhagen Airport jobs in restructuring
content.shortHeadline: Norwegian to cut 123 jobs at Copenhagen Airport
content.standfirst: The airline says 53 pilots and 70 cabin crew will lose their jobs as it adjusts its Copenhagen-based fleet to seasonal demand. The union says the move risks replacing Danish staff with cheaper Spanish labour; Norwegian says alternatives were rejected.

image.caption: Norwegian plans to reduce the number of aircraft based in Copenhagen during summer.

sources.originalTitle: Norwegian fyrer 123 ansatte i Københavns Lufthavn

segments.body: Norwegian has confirmed 123 redundancies among staff based at Copenhagen Airport: 53 pilots and 70 cabin crew. Most are expected to leave at the end of January, with the rest scheduled to go ten months later. The company plans to reduce its Copenhagen-based fleet in summer from 16 aircraft to 14.

segments.title: Dispute over alternatives
segments.body: Norwegian says seasonal contracts or voluntary leave could have reduced the number of redundancies, but the union was not willing to negotiate those options. Flyvebranchens Personale Union says the changes amount to an attempt to replace Danish employees with cheaper Spanish labour. Norwegian has not accepted that characterisation.

perspectives.body: The union’s account and the airline’s explanation differ: the union alleges a move towards cheaper Spanish labour, while Norwegian says it sought seasonal arrangements and voluntary leave to avoid some redundancies.

content.headline: Randers garden house must be demolished after final planning ruling
content.shortHeadline: Final ruling orders demolition of Randers garden house
content.standfirst: The appeals board says a recently built allotment house violates coastal-protection rules because it was constructed without a required exemption. The owner says she tried to follow the rules; neighbours fear similar decisions could affect other homes.

image.caption: Janne Lund’s allotment house in Randers is due to be demolished.

sources.originalTitle: Jannes nybyggede kolonihavehus er opført ulovligt: Nu skal det jævnes med jorden

segments.body: A final decision by Denmark’s Environmental and Food Appeals Board means Janne Lund must demolish her allotment house in the Venezuela garden association in Randers. The board found that the new building, completed in 2023, lacked a required exemption from the coastal-protection rules and was too large, high and prominent in the landscape.

segments.title: Neighbours fear wider consequences
segments.body: Lund says she sought guidance from the authorities and expects to lose about 1.5 million kroner as well as the retreat she built. Her neighbour, who says his own house also lacks an exemption, fears it could face the same outcome. The report says nearly 30 other allotment houses lie at a similar distance from the water; their legal status is not established here.

content.headline: Minister’s sick leave shifts SF’s role in Denmark’s government committees
content.shortHeadline: Signe Munk’s sick leave reshapes SF’s government roles
content.standfirst: Signe Munk’s absence moves former environment group leader Maria Reumert Gjerding into a key government economic committee, while Karina Lorentzen Denhardt takes Munk’s place on the green committee. The changes alter SF’s influence inside government.

image.caption: SF leader Pia Olsen Dyhr and Signe Munk at government negotiations in Marienborg.

sources.originalTitle: ANALYSE Pia Olsen Dyhr skal undvære sin makker fra Marienborg – til gengæld rykker en minister med kort SF-historie frem i bussen

segments.body: Signe Munk, the Socialist People’s Party’s city, rural and transport minister, has gone on sick leave. Maria Reumert Gjerding, formerly president of the Danish Society for Nature Conservation, will join the government’s economic committee and take a central role in the party’s green-policy work. Karina Lorentzen Denhardt will replace Munk on the green committee.

segments.title: A change in political weight
segments.body: DR’s analysis says Munk was an experienced figure in the government negotiations and a trusted partner of party leader Pia Olsen Dyhr. Gjerding’s new position gives her greater influence on environmental policy, while Munk’s absence removes a knowledgeable negotiator from the party’s internal team. The report does not give a reason or expected duration for the sick leave.

content.headline: Danish police reopen old abuse case and charge 65-year-old man
content.shortHeadline: Man charged in reopened case over alleged abuse of daughter
content.standfirst: East Jutland police say new information from a television programme prompted them to reopen a case and arrest a 65-year-old man. He denies the allegation; a court hearing on Wednesday will consider the prosecution’s request for custody.

image.caption: The 65-year-old man is charged over alleged offences from about 13 years ago.

sources.originalTitle: Mand sigtet for 13 år gamle overgreb på datter efter tv-program

segments.body: A 65-year-old man has been arrested and charged over alleged sexual abuse of one of his daughters about 13 years ago, East Jutland Police say. The alleged victim was about 12 at the time. Police say they reopened the case after receiving new information connected with a television programme.

segments.title: Allegation denied
segments.body: The man is due to appear in court in Randers, where prosecutors will seek to have him remanded in custody. His defence lawyer says the client unequivocally denies that abuse took place and argues he was put under significant pressure to confirm a particular account of the past during covert recordings. The allegation has not been tested in court.

content.headline: Appeal court upholds father’s sentence for sending daughters to Somalia
content.shortHeadline: Appeal court upholds sentence over daughters sent to Somalia
content.standfirst: A Danish appeals court has confirmed a three-year prison sentence imposed on a father for sending his three daughters to Somalia in 2022. The case is among a small number to result in a conviction under the law against harmful overseas stays.

sources.originalTitle: Landsret stadfæster dom for at sende døtre på genopdragelsesrejse

segments.body: The Western High Court has upheld a three-year prison sentence for a 57-year-old man who sent his daughters, then aged 7, 12 and 14, to Somalia in 2022 for what the report describes as a re-education trip. The original sentence was handed down by Aarhus District Court in April.

segments.title: Rare prosecutions
segments.body: The prosecution service says the case is among the few that have led to a conviction since it became illegal to send children abroad for stays that endanger their health and development. A report by research centre VIVE found an average of one such case a year since 2019.

content.headline: Four electrical products recalled over risk of electric shock
content.shortHeadline: Electrical products sold at Bilka and Føtex recalled
content.standfirst: EpiqApS is recalling four products, including extension leads, power strips and an adapter, sold at Bilka and Føtex from June to September. The company says the sockets lack child protection at the openings, creating a risk of electric shock.

sources.originalTitle: Ledningssæt med stikdåser tilbagekaldes - risiko for elektrisk stød

segments.body: EpiqApS has recalled four electrical products sold at Bilka and Føtex between 2 June and 18 September 2026. The recall includes extension-lead sets with three, four or five sockets and the Scoop double adapter. The company says the sockets do not have child protection at the openings, creating a risk of electric shock.

content.headline: Danish publishers draw different lines on AI use in book production
content.shortHeadline: Danish publishers set rules for AI in book production
content.standfirst: Several publishers restrict the use of external AI tools on manuscripts, citing copyright and authorship, while allowing some internal tools for other tasks. Their policies vary, and Gyldendal has not disclosed the details of its internal rules.

image.caption: Danish publishers are setting policies on the use of AI in book production.

sources.originalTitle: Hvor frit spil har AI på de danske forlag?

segments.body: Lindhardt og Ringhof says employees and external collaborators may not use external AI tools for work done for the publisher, though staff can use its internal tools. Gutkind says it avoids generative AI in editorial work but allows an internal tool for administrative and analytical tasks. Its director says the publisher will not monitor every use by translators.

segments.title: Different approaches
segments.body: Politikens Forlag says manuscript use of AI must be discussed with a manager and declared to the author, and that AI-made covers should be identified in the book. Gyldendal says it has internal rules and is discussing them with partners but has not produced written external guidelines. The publishers share a concern for authors’ rights, but describe different boundaries and enforcement.

content.headline: House prices rise sharply in five Danish areas beyond the largest cities
content.shortHeadline: House prices rise beyond Denmark’s biggest cities
content.standfirst: Data show notable price rises since 2013 in Lejre, Bornholm, Billund, Rebild and Svendborg. Local estate agents point to different drivers, including access to nature, jobs, holiday homes and commuters from larger cities.

sources.originalTitle: Glem København og Aarhus - her er fem kommuner, hvor huspriserne også stiger markant

segments.body: House prices in several areas outside Denmark’s largest cities have risen markedly since 2013, according to figures from Boligsiden. The report highlights Lejre, Bornholm, Billund, Rebild and Svendborg, where increases range from 61% in Svendborg to 112% in Lejre.

segments.title: Different local drivers
segments.body: Estate agents cited in the report point to different factors: buyers from Copenhagen and access to nature in Lejre; holiday-home demand on Bornholm; jobs linked to Lego in Billund; commuting and natural surroundings in Rebild; and coastal access and town life in Svendborg. These explanations are local agents’ assessments, not a single nationwide cause.

content.headline: David Bowie’s lost 1978 concert film is heading to arenas in 2027
content.shortHeadline: Bowie’s lost 1978 concert film is heading to arenas
content.standfirst: Director Brett Morgen spent years restoring footage of two Earl’s Court shows. The result will be presented as a multimedia arena event, with Bowie’s 1978 performance framed for a 2027 audience.

image.caption: David Bowie performing at Earl’s Court during the 1978 Isolar II tour.

sources.originalTitle: ‘How on earth is this man not sweating?’ The director who spent 10 years painstakingly remastering Bowie’s ‘greatest filmed performance’
‘Lost’ 1978 David Bowie tour film to play arenas in 2027, remastered by Moonage Daydream director Brett Morgen

segments.body: In 1978, David Bowie commissioned director David Hemmings to film two Earl’s Court concerts. The footage was never released, and Bowie later said he disliked how it had been shot. Brett Morgen discovered the 35mm film while working on his Bowie documentary, Moonage Daydream, and has spent years restoring it.

segments.title: From archive to arena
segments.body: The 2027 presentation, titled Stage, will use multiple screens, lighting and immersive sound rather than simply showing a concert film in a cinema. The shows capture Bowie and his band on the Isolar II tour, performing material from Low and “Heroes” alongside older songs. The project is due to premiere at the Berlin film festival in February before touring.

content.headline: Macklemore’s Dublin benefit show turns a tour into a collective statement
content.shortHeadline: Macklemore’s Dublin benefit show becomes a collective statement
content.standfirst: The first European date of the rapper’s Free Palestine tour brought together Hozier, Kneecap and other guests at a sold-out 3Arena. The review finds a show whose scale and purpose made it feel like more than a concert.

image.caption: Macklemore performing in Dublin on the Free Palestine tour.

sources.originalTitle: Macklemore’s Free Palestine tour review – a triumph of a show with performances from Hozier, Kneecap and more

segments.body: Macklemore’s sold-out Dublin show brought together local and international performers, activists and video-message guests, with proceeds from the tour going to organisations assisting Palestinians. Hozier, Kneecap, Beoga and Palestinian American DJ Habibeats were among those appearing, alongside messages from actors and musicians.

segments.title: The cause and the show
segments.body: The review describes a crowd with an “infectiously giddy excitement” and a bill that moved between music, advocacy and speeches. Kneecap’s chaotic set and Hozier’s audience-facing performance stood out; when Macklemore finally took the stage, the critic heard a renewed sense of purpose in his older hits as well as his newer material.

content.headline: Jack Antonoff stands by the love songs he wrote before his marriage ended
content.shortHeadline: Jack Antonoff stands by songs written before his marriage ended
content.standfirst: The Bleachers frontman says performing songs about his marriage after its breakdown has become a way to honour what he felt at the time. He also speaks candidly about grief, online criticism and the costs of touring.

image.caption: Jack Antonoff, second from right, with his band Bleachers.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I’d rather live through something publicly than escape it privately’: Jack Antonoff on survivor’s guilt and still singing love songs after his breakup

segments.body: Jack Antonoff decided not to change Bleachers’ setlist after his marriage ended, even though it includes songs written about that relationship. He says the choice reflects the honesty he owes his audience: he does not want to rewrite the past, and has found that singing the material can be meaningful for both him and listeners.

segments.title: An unusually candid pop career
segments.body: The interview also explores the tension between Antonoff’s confessional work with Bleachers and his role as a producer for major pop stars. He discusses the death of his sister and what he calls survivor’s guilt, criticises the experience of buying concert tickets through Live Nation, and says he feels emboldened to speak in support of Palestine at shows.

content.headline: Manic Street Preachers revisit the weight of The Holy Bible and Richey Edwards
content.shortHeadline: Manic Street Preachers face the legacy of The Holy Bible
content.standfirst: James Dean Bradfield reflects on performing the band’s 1994 album in full, its difficult lyrics and the disappearance of lyricist Richey Edwards. A newly released live recording preserves the group’s attempt to meet their past directly.

image.caption: James Dean Bradfield, Nicky Wire and Sean Moore of Manic Street Preachers.

sources.originalTitle: Manic Street Preachers: ‘We just weren’t equipped to deal with Richey’s problems’

segments.body: Manic Street Preachers’ new live album captures their 2014 performances of The Holy Bible, the dark and politically confrontational record whose lyrics were chiefly written by Richey Edwards. Edwards disappeared in 1995 and was legally declared dead in 2008. For Bradfield, revisiting the songs meant confronting their language and the absence that has shaped the band ever since.

segments.title: What the songs still ask
segments.body: Bradfield says the album is not simply a collection of horrors: some songs show empathy for people living with eating disorders and the victims of war. He also recalls how the band, young and unequipped to respond to Edwards’s deteriorating mental health, now wonders whether they should have stopped him touring. The anniversary performances were difficult, he says, but the band felt they had done the record justice.

content.headline: Jay-Z will headline the 2027 Super Bowl halftime show he helped produce
content.shortHeadline: Jay-Z will headline the 2027 Super Bowl halftime show
content.standfirst: After years of helping Roc Nation produce the NFL’s halftime entertainment, the rapper will take the stage himself at Super Bowl LXI in California. The announcement follows a recent run of concerts at the same stadium.

image.caption: Jay-Z performing in Paris.

sources.originalTitle: Jay-Z picks headliner for 2027 Super Bowl half-time show … Jay-Z

segments.body: Jay-Z has been named the featured performer at the 2027 Super Bowl halftime show, scheduled for 14 February at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California. His company Roc Nation has partnered with the NFL on entertainment production since 2019. NFL commissioner Roger Goodell said he had hoped Jay-Z would perform one day.

The announcement marks a change from Jay-Z’s earlier reluctance to perform at the event: when Roc Nation began working with the NFL, he said that if the agreement was about him taking the stage, the conversation could end. The 56-year-old has not released a solo album since 2017, but the report notes his extensive catalogue and recent concerts at SoFi Stadium.

content.headline: Neil Young sues Trump’s political action committee again over his song
content.shortHeadline: Neil Young sues Trump’s PAC over “Rockin’ in the Free World”
content.standfirst: Young is seeking $10 million in a new copyright lawsuit over the song’s use at Donald Trump’s rallies. The filing says a 2020 settlement promised the track would not be used again without permission.

image.caption: Neil Young in 2019.

sources.originalTitle: Neil Young files second lawsuit against Trump for unauthorised use of Rockin’ in the Free World at rallies

segments.body: Neil Young has filed a second lawsuit over the use of “Rockin’ in the Free World” at Donald Trump’s political rallies, this time naming the Trump 47 Committee. The suit, filed in federal court in Virginia, seeks $10 million in reputational damages and an injunction against further public performances.

segments.title: A dispute that has returned
segments.body: Young’s first case, filed in 2020 against another Trump organisation, was settled. The new suit says that organisation promised not to use the song again without a licence and permission. It cites the song’s use at an Ohio rally on 12 October and alleges it was played at other rallies. The Trump administration had not responded to the suit at the time of the report.

content.headline: Caroline Rose turns suburban oddballs into punk-fuelled comedy
content.shortHeadline: Caroline Rose’s new album makes room for suburban oddballs
content.standfirst: On their seventh album, the singer-songwriter embraces the anarchic, funny side of their writing, pairing fast, distorted songs with portraits of misfits and strained lives. The review hears a record that is both gleefully absurd and unexpectedly tender.

sources.originalTitle: Gentling the Horse at the Walt Whitman Mall

segments.body: Caroline Rose’s Gentling the Horse at the Walt Whitman Mall returns to “Yip Yip Yow,” a song they first performed in 2015 and later released as a single. The new version is louder and rougher, setting the tone for an album that trades the melancholy of their previous record for gutter-punk guitars, speed and a deliberately unruly sense of humour.

segments.title: Funny, but not weightless
segments.body: The review finds Rose’s cartoonish cast of suburban outsiders funny without making their troubles disposable. “Conversation with Shiv” looks back on a friendship marked by drug use and money problems, while the album’s title reflects Rose’s bemusement at a shopping centre named for the queer poet Walt Whitman. Under the jokes, the critic hears a portrait of people living at the margins of a capitalist society.

content.headline: Tony Iommi finds a forceful new voice for his return to solo metal
content.shortHeadline: Tony Iommi’s return to solo work goes back to metal basics
content.standfirst: The Black Sabbath guitarist’s first solo album in more than two decades pairs his heavy riffs with Norwegian singer Jørn Lande. Pitchfork’s review calls it Iommi’s strongest work under his own name.

sources.originalTitle: From the Dark

segments.body: On From the Dark, Tony Iommi returns to solo work with a heavy-metal record fronted by Norwegian vocalist Jørn Lande. The review hears a deliberate choice to avoid both a proposed final Black Sabbath album and the blues-rock direction of Iommi’s earlier collaborations with singer Glenn Hughes.

segments.title: A partnership built around the riffs
segments.body: The critic praises Iommi’s controlled, weighty guitar work and describes Lande’s performance as a career best, while noting that his admiration for Ronnie James Dio is audible. The review’s main reservation is Brian May’s guest solo on “Death Wake,” which it finds less distinctive than another lead from Iommi might have been.

content.headline: Elon Musk’s AI-made Odyssey is a hollow answer to Christopher Nolan’s film
content.shortHeadline: Musk’s AI-made Odyssey is a hollow answer to Nolan’s
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s review of Grok’s seven-minute Homer adaptation finds ponderous animation, flat performances and no real dramatic purpose. Its main value, the critic argues, is showing the gulf between generating images and making art.

image.caption: A still from the AI-generated Odyssey episode made with Grok.

sources.originalTitle: Elon Musk’s AI Odyssey review – the dullest, most pointless riposte possible to Christopher Nolan’s brilliant epic

segments.body: Elon Musk has released a seven-minute opening episode of an Odyssey made with Grok AI, after objecting online to Christopher Nolan’s version and claiming he could make a more authentic adaptation. The Guardian’s critic describes the result as an inert prologue, with computer-generated imagery and even-toned, robotic dialogue.

segments.title: A question of artistic value
segments.body: The review argues that the episode’s dramatic events—Odysseus leaving his family and joining the war, among them—feel motiveless, and that the work seems driven more by a wish to win an online argument than to tell Homer’s story. The critic allows that later episodes could improve, but says this first one highlights the difference between AI’s potential financial value and its artistic merit.

content.headline: We, the Hated captures the backlash and dilemmas of Just Stop Oil protests
content.shortHeadline: A documentary follows Just Stop Oil into hostile protests
content.standfirst: Rich Felgate’s film records activists facing abuse and violence while campaigning through disruptive direct action. The review sees the group’s purpose and the public’s anger, while questioning whether its tactics alienate the people it hopes to persuade.

image.caption: A scene from We, the Hated, filmed close to Just Stop Oil protests.

sources.originalTitle: We, the Hated review – standing up to be abused: behind the scenes with Just Stop Oil

segments.body: We, the Hated follows Just Stop Oil protests from close range, with director Rich Felgate filming among activists, including his girlfriend, Indigo Rumbelow. The footage shows road blockades, confrontations with drivers and arrests; the review describes verbal abuse and physical aggression directed at protesters.

segments.title: The cost of disruption
segments.body: The film gives activists space to argue that climate action cannot wait, while also showing hostile TV interviews and public frustration with tactics that inconvenience ordinary people. The critic says targeting infrastructure rather than the fossil-fuel industry can squander goodwill. Activists’ prison sentences and the campaign’s claimed political gains leave the film asking who bears responsibility for the conflict.

content.headline: City of Masks turns a West End theatre into a muddled ghost romance
content.shortHeadline: City of Masks is a muddled West End ghost story
content.standfirst: A young actor is coached by the ghost of a composer who died in the theatre where he is performing. The Guardian’s review likes Amanda Jiang’s mysterious presence but finds the film’s romance and plot increasingly baffling.

image.caption: Amanda Jiang as Eve in City of Masks.

sources.originalTitle: City of Masks review – theatreland ghost story with female phantom of the opera out for revenge

segments.body: In City of Masks, earnest actor Christian begins hearing the voice of Eve, a composer who died in a fire at the West End theatre now staging her musical. The film turns the Phantom of the Opera setup on its head, with a female ghost coaching a male performer as questions gather around the old fire.

segments.title: A haunted production
segments.body: The review praises Amanda Jiang’s sensual, mysterious performance as Eve but finds a clash between her style and the director character’s heightened intensity. As the suspected cause of the fire becomes part of the story and Christian develops feelings for Eve, the critic says the ghost-on-human romance grows uncomfortable and the plot harder to follow.

content.headline: You Can See Everything’s audience is still deciding what kind of film it is
content.shortHeadline: Audiences leave You Can See Everything unsure what to think
content.standfirst: At a sold-out New York screening, viewers laughed, murmured and sometimes fell silent during Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary. The Guardian finds that its unsettled audience response is part of the film’s growing appeal.

image.caption: Advertising for You Can See Everything.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A cultural moment’: smash hit doc You Can See Everything continues to dazzle America

segments.body: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s three-hour documentary You Can See Everything has become a substantial cinema hit. At a sold-out Times Square screening, the Guardian’s reporter watched a young audience respond with laughter, discomfort and uncertainty to a film that moves between the convicted Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes and the people around her.

segments.title: An audience in the mirror
segments.body: Viewers told the reporter that social-media clips and word of mouth had made the film feel like a cultural event, while many arrived without knowing its mid-film turn. Reactions ranged from sympathy for Holmes to suspicion of her account. The story asks whether this appetite signals audiences are ready for difficult cinema, or whether a documentary built around familiar TV figures gets more leeway than a conventional drama.

content.headline: Bad Day at the Office is a frantic first-person thriller that overstays its run
content.shortHeadline: Bad Day at the Office is a frantic thriller that wears you out
content.standfirst: John Hannah races through gangland London in a GoPro-shot action comedy full of parkour, absurd props and cartoonish violence. The Guardian enjoys its uninhibited energy but says the film’s 111 minutes outlast the novelty.

image.caption: John Hannah in Bad Day at the Office.

sources.originalTitle: Bad Day at the Office review – gratuitously entertaining Go-Pro thriller is like Crank meets The Hangover

segments.body: John Hannah plays Karl Davis, who wakes with amnesia in a trashed hotel room beside a dead body and soon finds himself dodging gangsters and fake police. Director Chee Keong Cheung shoots much of Bad Day at the Office from a first-person perspective, pushing the action through a hectic stream of parkour, fights and graphic on-screen annotations.

segments.title: Novelty at full speed
segments.body: The review calls the result “kind of glorious” in its delirious first stretch, as Karl scrambles across rooftops and fights his way through London’s underworld. But it finds that the gimmick loses force when the film returns to familiar revenge plotting, and argues that the relentless 111-minute pace makes the experience feel much longer.

content.headline: November’s film slate ranges from Ian Charleson’s Hamlet to Hunger Games
content.shortHeadline: November films: Ian Charleson’s Hamlet and a new Hunger Games
content.standfirst: The month’s cinema and streaming releases include Andrew Scott as actor Ian Charleson, another Hunger Games prequel and a new film from Ryusuke Hamaguchi. This guide gathers the titles and release dates to watch.

sources.originalTitle: Elsinore to The Hunger Games: 12 of the best films to watch in November

segments.body: November’s film releases range from Elsinore, in which Andrew Scott plays actor Ian Charleson as he takes on Hamlet while living with AIDS, to Sunrise on the Reaping, a new Hunger Games prequel. The guide also highlights Club Kid, a comedy-drama about a New York party promoter who meets the son he did not know he had.

segments.title: More to look out for
segments.body: The selection also includes Siân Heder’s disability-rights drama Being Heumann, a new film from Ryusuke Hamaguchi, and the animated fantasy Hexed. The guide provides cinema and streaming release dates across several territories, making it a useful browse for readers planning what to see next month.

content.headline: The Dropout is finding a new audience after You Can See Everything
content.shortHeadline: You Can See Everything is sending viewers back to The Dropout
content.standfirst: A new Elizabeth Holmes documentary has driven renewed interest in the 2022 TV drama and the podcast that preceded it. The Guardian argues that the older series still offers a bracing account of Theranos’s claims and their consequences.

image.caption: Amanda Seyfried and Naveen Andrews in The Dropout.

sources.originalTitle: Elizabeth Holmes mania: how the buzziest film of the year has resurrected a gut-twisting TV drama

segments.body: The success of You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, has sent viewers back to The Dropout. The Guardian reports that the Disney/Hulu series’ audience rose sharply after the film’s release, alongside a surge in listeners for the podcast of the same name.

segments.title: Beyond the spectacle
segments.body: The article contrasts the documentary’s open questions about Holmes’s self-presentation with The Dropout’s account of Theranos’s failed blood-testing claims, its workplace culture and the harm caused by unreliable results. Amanda Seyfried’s performance remains part of the series’ appeal, but the renewed attention also brings the company’s underlying facts back into view.

content.headline: The One About Matthew Perry makes a warm, unflinching tribute
content.shortHeadline: The One About Matthew Perry is a tender, candid tribute
content.standfirst: This three-part documentary draws on interviews with Perry’s family, friends and former partners to tell the story of his rise, addiction and death. The Guardian finds intimacy and generosity in a portrait that also speaks to those who loved him.

image.caption: Matthew Perry.

sources.originalTitle: The One About Matthew Perry review – the star of one of TV’s biggest ever shows gets a loving tribute

segments.body: The One About Matthew Perry follows the actor from his early years in Los Angeles to his fame on Friends and his death in 2023, aged 54. Family members, close friends and former partners describe him with evident affection, while the documentary does not sidestep the addiction that shaped his later life.

segments.title: A private grief, shared
segments.body: The review says the three-hour film is moving because its contributors speak about Perry as a person, not only as a star. Their memories of repeated attempts to get sober and the pain of watching him relapse lend the tribute a wider resonance for families affected by addiction, without turning the story into an easy or simple tragedy.

content.headline: Escaping Idi Amin recalls Asian Ugandans’ expulsion through survivors’ memories
content.shortHeadline: Escaping Idi Amin follows survivors of Uganda’s Asian expulsion
content.standfirst: Four people who were children in Uganda describe the violence and fear surrounding Idi Amin’s 1972 order that the country’s Asian population leave within 90 days. The Guardian finds their testimony an urgent account of displacement and refuge.

image.caption: A reconstruction of Harminder Singh and his father’s escape from Uganda to Britain.

sources.originalTitle: Escaping Idi Amin review – there’s a happy ending to this awful tale … and it should be a lesson to us all

segments.body: The two-part documentary Escaping Idi Amin hears from four people who grew up in Uganda and later became British citizens. They recall how the 1972 order forced around 80,000 Asian Ugandans to leave the country within 90 days, after Amin’s government had taken power and begun targeting its opponents.

segments.title: A question of refuge
segments.body: The review places the survivors’ memories alongside the hostility that greeted the prospect of their arrival in Britain, despite many holding British passports. It describes the family flight and the new lives they built after leaving Uganda, while arguing that the documentary’s account of scapegoating and asylum still has relevance beyond the events it records.

content.headline: Miranda Hart’s warmth becomes the heart of The Celebrity Traitors
content.shortHeadline: Miranda Hart brings warmth and laughter to The Celebrity Traitors
content.standfirst: The i Paper argues that Hart’s kindness, physical comedy and openness have become the standout qualities of this celebrity series. Her departure also prompted a rare moment of reflection on laughter, connection and returning to work after illness.

image.caption: Miranda Hart in The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Miranda has brought wholesome joy back to TV

segments.body: The i Paper’s review of The Celebrity Traitors focuses on Miranda Hart, whose playful moments—from a mistaken “Big Mix” dance lesson to slapstick challenges—have become some of the series’ most widely shared scenes. The writer says Hart has brought a warmth to a programme otherwise built around suspicion, banishment and bluff.

segments.title: A return to the screen
segments.body: After her exit, Hart spoke about how the show let her reconnect with work and with other people after years of chronic fatigue syndrome. The review sees that candour as part of her comic appeal: she is willing to be vulnerable and not take herself too seriously, making the series’ language of laughter and connection feel more than a game.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future leaves fans and the BBC waiting
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after its latest run
content.standfirst: With no new Doctor announced, a planned Christmas special cancelled and the BBC’s Disney+ partnership ended, the series faces an uncertain pause. A reported history of its revivals shows why fans and industry observers disagree on what should come next.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, including Ncuti Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Doctor Who has been off air since the 2025 series starring Ncuti Gatwa. The BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+, cancelled a planned Christmas special and put future production out to competitive tender, with no new Doctor announced. The corporation has declined interview requests, leaving questions about the show’s next chapter unanswered.

segments.title: A history of reinvention
segments.body: The feature traces how the series has repeatedly renewed itself, from its 2005 return after a 16-year break to successive changes of lead actor and showrunner. Some contributors blame weaker scripts and confusing storytelling for recent audience losses; others argue the show can recover if it returns to its core values and preserves the character’s established world. No single cause or solution is settled.

content.headline: Eight indie horror games offer everything from cursed cards to Antarctic penguin
content.shortHeadline: Eight indie horror games for Halloween, from penguins to devils
content.standfirst: A seasonal guide ranges across eerie adventures, occult card battles and low-budget interactive horror. Its picks include The Killing Stone, Silver Pines and Tenebris Somnia, alongside an Antarctic exploration game starring a penguin.

image.caption: A scene from The Killing Stone.

sources.originalTitle: Eight great new indie horror games for Halloween

segments.body: For Halloween, the Guardian rounds up eight independent horror releases, from an illustrated point-and-click fairy tale to Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival. The selection also includes a Scottish takeaway horror made with Gaelic dialogue and a 17th-century witch-hunt adventure, showing how broadly small-scale games are exploring the genre.

segments.title: Different kinds of fear
segments.body: Among the other picks are The Killing Stone, a card game set in a remote mansion, Silver Pines, a puzzle-filled mystery in an abandoned town, and Tenebris Somnia, which combines pixel art with live-action sequences. The guide also points readers towards Penguin Colony, an Antarctic exploration game in which a penguin observes Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors.

content.headline: BioWare’s closure and cancelled Mass Effect leave fans mourning a lost RPG world
content.shortHeadline: BioWare’s closure leaves Mass Effect fans grieving a lost future
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s contributor reflects on EA’s announcement that the studio is closing and its planned Mass Effect game has been cancelled, with more than 400 jobs lost. The news lands particularly hard for players who found lasting meaning in the original trilogy.

image.caption: A scene from Mass Effect 3.

sources.originalTitle: EA has closed BioWare – and Mass Effect fans like me are bereft

segments.body: EA has announced the closure of BioWare, cancelling its forthcoming Mass Effect game and putting more than 400 jobs at risk, according to the Guardian article. The writer, a games-industry veteran and long-time fan, describes the studio’s loss as a major blow to role-playing games and to players waiting for another story in the series.

segments.title: Why the trilogy endured
segments.body: The writer recalls how Mass Effect’s character relationships and consequential choices made a familiar mission to save the galaxy feel personal. Decisions carried across the trilogy, shaping the fate of characters and entire communities. That history helps explain the sense of loss, even as the article acknowledges BioWare’s recent struggles to produce a critical or commercial hit.

content.headline: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 balances explosive set pieces with character
content.shortHeadline: Modern Warfare 4 makes its battles serve the story
content.standfirst: A review praises the new campaign’s pace and spectacle, while a developer interview explains how Infinity Ward tried to make its missions and characters work together. The game’s political setting and its treatment of player choice remain part of the discussion.

image.caption: A scene from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.

sources.originalTitle: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 review – a thrilling airport novel of a game
‘The audience gets to be in on it’: How narrative-led gameplay is Call of Duty’s greatest weapon

segments.body: The Guardian’s review calls Modern Warfare 4 a polished, fast-moving campaign, moving from parkour across Manhattan rooftops to a battle at a North Korean airbase. It also notes quieter sections and moments that force players into ethically stark actions, while criticising the ending for giving Captain Price’s story less weight than intended.

segments.title: Building action around people
segments.body: In a separate interview, narrative director Jeff Negus describes how Infinity Ward sought to make large-scale action matter by first establishing the people caught in it. The team used military and cultural consultants, including a dialect coach familiar with differences between North and South Korean speech, and tested and rearranged story beats during development.

content.headline: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort makes family gaming an easy group activity
content.shortHeadline: Switch Sports Resort is built for easy family fun
content.standfirst: Nintendo’s new collection adds seven activities to familiar sports, from archery and skateboarding to jetskiing. The Guardian’s reviewer finds it welcoming for children and adults, with a lively island setting that gives solo play more to explore.

image.caption: A scene from Nintendo Switch Sports Resort.

sources.originalTitle: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort review – Wii Sports lives on in this effortlessly appealing collection of games

segments.body: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort brings back tennis, bowling and volleyball, adds golf and basketball, and introduces seven new activities including boxing, archery, skateboarding and jetskiing. The review finds most of them intuitive to pick up, with enough silliness to make the collection work well for family play.

segments.title: A place to return to
segments.body: The game’s island can be explored by jetski or plane, with beaches, stadiums and small details visible along the way. Unlockable outfits, sport variations and obstacle courses add reasons to keep playing outside the main events. The reviewer says the package became a fixture at home, sustaining both group sessions and a child’s interest over time.

content.headline: Personalised mRNA vaccine cuts melanoma recurrence risk in phase III trial
content.shortHeadline: Personalised mRNA vaccine cuts melanoma recurrence risk
content.standfirst: In a large trial, adding a patient-specific vaccine to pembrolizumab lowered the two-year risk of melanoma returning or death. The treatment still needs further study and regulatory review before routine use.

image.caption: Melanoma researcher Georgina Long, who described the trial findings as a major shift towards personalised cancer treatment.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Bespoke’ mRNA vaccine significantly reduces risk of melanoma recurrence or death, clinical trial shows

segments.body: The Australian-led phase III trial enrolled 1,137 people whose melanoma had been surgically removed but was considered at high risk of returning. Everyone received pembrolizumab; some also received intismeran, an mRNA vaccine designed around mutations in their own tumour. At two years, the combination group had a 42% lower risk of recurrence or death than the group receiving pembrolizumab alone.

segments.title: What remains to be established
segments.body: After two years, 82% of those given the combination were alive and free of recurrence, compared with 70% of those treated with pembrolizumab alone. Researchers say longer follow-up is needed to assess survival and how durable the benefit will be. The vaccine is not yet a standard treatment and may not help everyone; further study and regulatory review are still required.

content.headline: Optogenetic treatment restores useful vision in six of 10 patients
content.shortHeadline: Light-based gene therapy restores some vision in six patients
content.standfirst: A small trial used gene therapy to make retinal cells respond to amber light, helping some people with advanced retinitis pigmentosa perform simple tasks. The approach is experimental and does not restore normal sight.

image.caption: Optogenetics uses light to control nerve-cell activity.

sources.originalTitle: A cure for blindness is coming

segments.body: Optogenetics uses light to switch nerve cells on or off. In a study of 10 people with severe sight loss from retinitis pigmentosa, researchers delivered a gene to the retina so some cells would respond to amber light; patients wore special glasses that converted ordinary light. After three months, six participants had improved enough to complete tasks such as picking up a cup.

segments.title: A limited, early result
segments.body: The treatment did not restore normal vision. Participants first perceived dots of light and had to learn to interpret them; they could not distinguish faces. Researchers are working on approaches that might provide more detail. Optogenetics is also being explored for conditions including pain, epilepsy and deafness, but those applications remain at earlier stages and some would require gene therapy that may be irreversible.

content.headline: Scientists recreate the colour-changing effect of ancient Roman glass
content.shortHeadline: Scientists recreate Roman glass that changes colour in light
content.standfirst: Researchers at the University of Sheffield have reproduced the green-to-red optical effect of the fourth-century Lycurgus Cup using gold and silver nanoparticles. The work may help explain how Roman glassmakers achieved the striking colours.

image.caption: The Lycurgus Cup appears green in ordinary light and red when lit from behind.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s magic’: scientists rediscover how to make ancient Roman colour-changing glass

segments.body: The Lycurgus Cup appears jade green in ordinary light and ruby red when illuminated from behind. Researchers at the University of Sheffield have replicated the effect using an ancient recipe derived from a fragment of Roman glass, embedding tiny gold and silver nanocrystals in glass as it cooled.

segments.title: How the effect works
segments.body: The nanoparticles interact with light in different ways: light passing through the glass is filtered so reds and oranges show through, while light reflected from its surface is scattered to produce an opaque green. Archaeological materials expert Ian Freestone said the Sheffield work comes closer to the original colours than a previous 1960s replica. He noted that furnace conditions could have made the effect difficult for Roman craftspeople to control.

content.headline: A fertile Cavendish banana opens a new route to disease-resistant fruit
content.shortHeadline: Fertile Cavendish banana may open a route to disease resistance
content.standfirst: A research partnership says it has developed a fertile Cavendish line, potentially making cross-breeding possible for the usually sterile fruit. The details remain undisclosed, and any new variety would still need to meet growers’ tests for taste, yield and disease resistance.

image.caption: A researcher works on the banana-breeding programme aimed at tackling crop disease.

sources.originalTitle: Have scientists finally found a way to save the banana from disaster?

segments.body: Most commercial Cavendish bananas are grown from offshoots and are nearly genetically identical, leaving crops vulnerable to diseases such as Tropical Race 4. Yelloway, a collaboration between Chiquita and crop-improvement company KeyGene, says it has developed a fully fertile Cavendish line, which could allow breeders to cross it with other bananas.

segments.title: A possible route, not a finished solution
segments.body: Yelloway has not disclosed how the line was produced or how many chromosomes it has. Researchers say crossing it with disease-resistant bananas could yield useful offspring, but the fruit might differ substantially from Cavendish. Any candidate would still need to resist disease, produce high yields and taste acceptable. Other approaches include gene editing and a genetically modified Cavendish already approved for consumption in Australia and New Zealand.

content.headline: Climate change is prompting research into new crops for British farms
content.shortHeadline: New crops could help British farms adapt to hotter, drier summers
content.standfirst: Researchers are testing drought-tolerant crops such as lupins and chickpeas as heat and dry conditions affect familiar harvests. Their suitability for British farming still needs to be tested across varieties, locations and seasons.

image.caption: A lupin bhaji made with a crop researchers are exploring for warmer, drier conditions.

sources.originalTitle: The protein-packed superfoods of the future – that you could grow in your garden

segments.body: This year’s hot, dry summer harmed yields of crops including wheat, barley, broccoli, peas and potatoes, according to the reporting. Researchers at Southampton University are working with farmers, food companies and chefs to investigate alternatives that might suit a warmer, drier Britain, including lupins and chickpeas.

segments.title: Testing the alternatives
segments.body: Lupins are drought-tolerant and their beans can be processed into flour; chickpeas may also cope well with dry conditions. But researchers say they need to establish where crops grow best and how varieties perform, including their vulnerability to pests and disease, before farmers plant them at scale. Gardeners may also see shifts in which fruits and vegetables thrive in different parts of the UK.

content.headline: Embryo screening for a ‘best baby’ revives questions about eugenics
content.shortHeadline: The debate over embryo screening and the ‘best baby’ returns
content.standfirst: Commercial promises to screen IVF embryos for traits such as height and intelligence raise old questions in a new, consumer-led form. The essay argues that population-level genetic estimates cannot reliably predict an individual child’s future.

sources.originalTitle: Would you pay to have the ‘best baby’? Liberal eugenics and the troubling quest for human perfection

segments.body: The essay examines Nucleus Genomics’ marketing of IVF screening for genetic disorders and traits including eye colour, strength and intelligence. It argues that selling a “best baby” draws on the language of personal choice and self-improvement, while reviving a wider question: who decides which traits are desirable, and what that implies for people whose lives do not fit the ideal?

segments.title: What the numbers can—and cannot—say
segments.body: The company’s claims about how much height or intelligence is genetic refer to estimates of variation across populations, not a reliable way to choose how tall or intelligent an individual child will be. The essay notes that these estimates are contested and warns against treating statistical patterns as precise forecasts for a particular embryo.

segments.title: A disability perspective
segments.body: The author, who writes from personal experience of disability and a mistaken childhood diagnosis, distinguishes the desire for treatment from the idea that only a cured or optimised life is worth living. The essay argues for changing societies to accommodate human variation, rather than pursuing a single ideal of embodiment.

content.headline: UK flu season has started early, but that does not predict a worse winter
content.shortHeadline: Early flu activity is no guarantee of a severe season
content.standfirst: UK flu infections are rising earlier than usual, prompting health officials to urge eligible people to get vaccinated. Experts say the timing alone cannot tell us how severe the season will be.

image.caption: Flu activity is rising earlier than usual in the UK.

sources.originalTitle: Why so many people are sick right now

segments.body: Flu activity in the UK has begun rising in October, earlier than the usual winter peak. Experts say timing varies from year to year, and an early start does not necessarily mean a more severe season: last year’s activity also began early but overall flu deaths were below average.

segments.title: Why timing varies
segments.body: Possible explanations include changes in circulating flu strains, conditions that help viruses spread, and shifts in how people mix indoors. The mix of strains circulating in the Southern Hemisphere can offer clues about what may arrive in the UK, but it cannot settle how the season will unfold. The UK Health Security Agency is urging people eligible for an NHS flu vaccine to take it up.

content.headline: Hackers are exploiting critical PHP vulnerabilities, US agency warns
content.shortHeadline: Hackers are now exploiting critical PHP flaws
content.standfirst: After AI-assisted research helped uncover two long-hidden PHP bugs, the US cybersecurity agency CISA says attackers are exploiting them. The warning raises fresh pressure on organisations to patch vulnerable systems.

sources.originalTitle: US government says hackers are now exploiting critical PHP web bugs

segments.body: CISA says hackers are actively exploiting two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language used by many web-facing systems. The bugs can allow remote access to vulnerable systems without a password. The warning comes less than a week after patches were released and adds urgency to the earlier global response.

segments.title: Why the risk has changed
segments.body: Researchers initially said a working exploit would be difficult, though possible. The vulnerabilities had remained unpatched after maintainers judged them impractical to exploit; researchers later found a way to do so with help from an AI model. CISA did not identify the attackers in its warning. The report says the episode illustrates how AI can help surface and exploit flaws in older, under-resourced software.

content.headline: US Space Force gives SpaceX access to its most precise orbital tracking data
content.shortHeadline: SpaceX gains access to sensitive US orbital tracking data
content.standfirst: The military has given SpaceX enhanced access to detailed tracking information on objects in orbit, while receiving data from the company’s own system. Critics say the arrangement could deepen the firm’s advantage in an industry already reliant on its services.

image.caption: SpaceX’s facility in Hawthorne, California.

sources.originalTitle: US military gives Elon Musk’s SpaceX access to sensitive tracking data

segments.body: The US Space Force has given SpaceX access to a high-accuracy catalogue that includes tracking data from military sensors, telescopes and radar. The information can track objects as small as about 10cm in low Earth orbit. SpaceX’s Stargaze system uses cameras and radar mounted on Starlink satellites, but the military data is more precise.

segments.title: Safety and oversight concerns
segments.body: The military says it is exchanging commercial data for access to parts of the controlled, unclassified catalogue and is engaging with several companies. Industry observers warn that giving SpaceX access could widen its advantage in space traffic coordination as government plans for a public service remain unsettled. A former NOAA official quoted in the report says the deeper problem is the government’s failure to establish a clear, transparent framework for space governance.

content.headline: Data centre opposition is reshaping US election campaigns
content.shortHeadline: Data centre backlash is reshaping US election campaigns
content.standfirst: Candidates in several close US races are proposing pauses, tighter rules or local control as communities object to data centres’ demands on power, water and land. The issue is also attracting substantial political spending.

sources.originalTitle: Data center backlash is uniting America
Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing

segments.body: The rapid expansion of data centres has turned local concerns about electricity bills, water use and land into a campaign issue across the US. The BBC reports that the country has thousands of data centres and that their power demand is drawing pressure on local grids; supporters argue the facilities are important to AI, investment and national security.

segments.title: From local dispute to campaign pledge
segments.body: Candidates are taking varied positions, from temporary moratoriums to requirements that developers pay for power and water infrastructure. In Pennsylvania, for example, both candidates have shifted their public emphasis amid opposition, while polls cited in the reporting show many voters concerned about the effects of AI data centres. The competing proposals and changing positions reflect a debate over who bears the costs and who benefits.

content.headline: UK data centre plans face scrutiny over consultation and local impact
content.shortHeadline: UK data centre plans face scrutiny over consultation
content.standfirst: An investigation says UK officials met many businesses while developing data-centre policy but no environmental groups. Separately, residents in north Devon have protested a proposed large AI campus before a planning application has been submitted.
